title: Tipos de respaldo
description: Backup and data protection methods with speed trade-offs and archive bit behavior.
rows: Full
All selected data, every time.
Slowest backup / fastest restore (one set).
Clears the archive bit. Baseline that incremental and differential backups depend on.
Incremental
Data changed since the last backup of any type (full or incremental).
Fastest backup / slowest restore (last full plus every incremental in order).
Clears the archive bit. Losing one incremental in the chain breaks later restores.
Differential
Data changed since the last full backup.
Backup gets slower as the week goes on / restore needs only the last full plus the latest differential.
Does NOT clear the archive bit, so each differential grows until the next full.
Snapshot
Point-in-time image of a volume, VM, or storage system state.
Near-instant to create / fast rollback.
Often stored on the same system, so pair with copies elsewhere. Common for VMs and before changes.
Replication
Continuous or scheduled copying of data to another system or site.
Ongoing / near-immediate availability at the target.
Supports very low RPOs, but faithfully replicates corruption or ransomware encryption too; it is not a substitute for backups.
Journaling
Log of every change written before it is applied.
Low overhead / allows replay or rollback to a precise point.
Lets you recover to a moment just before corruption; used by file systems and databases.
Onsite
Backups kept at the same location as the source.
Fastest access for restores.
Vulnerable to the same fire, flood, or theft that hits the primary site.
Offsite
Backups stored at a separate location or in the cloud.
Slower to retrieve / survives a site-wide disaster.
Consider distance, transport security, and encryption. Industry often summarizes this as the 3-2-1 rule (three copies, two media, one offsite).
Encryption of backups
Protects backup media and files at rest and in transit.
Small overhead / requires the keys at restore time.
Losing the keys means losing the backup; manage keys separately from the data.
Recovery testing
Restoring backups to verify they actually work.
Not applicable.
A backup that has never been restored is unverified; test restores regularly.
